newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Malaysia fights cocoa pest with parasite.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia fights cocoa pest with parasite.

text.p: Malaysia plans to raise commercially a minute parasite wasp that can overwhelm the dreaded cocoa pod borer moth and be used to battle pests that affect corn and vegetables, an agronomist said on Wednesday.
Lee Ming Tong, deputy director-general of the Malaysian Cocoa Board, said field trials with Trichogramma, a wasp smaller than the tip of a pin, had produced excellent results.
"Field trials have shown that the cocoa yield loss can be reduced from as high as 80 percent to a mere five percent by the parasites," he told Reuters in an interview.
He said the use of Trichogramma was a relatively new technique, although it was a common parasite in the region.
Indonesia, the world's third largest cocoa producer after the Ivory Coast and Ghana, has been battling the cocoa pod borer for decades.

Lee was among 50 representatives from the government and private sectors of members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) who attended a two-day meeting to discuss the setting up of a regional cocoa trading contract.
The conference, which ended on Wednesday, agreed on the need to set up the contract, which delegates said was intended to reduce the region's dependence on foreign pacts.
Lee said the tiny wasp laid its eggs on the eggs of the pod borer moth, and its new-born penetrates the shell and feeds on the contents of the moth eggs.
The parasites were raised in the laboratory by letting them hatch and feed on the eggs of rice moths, he added.
He said 9.2 million wasps would be released in one hectare of cocoa plantings per year.
"So many are released because we want the parasite to be in the field the whole year round," he said.

"We are at the moment looking at the commercial rearing of the parasite by passing on the technology to the private sector, which can produce the wasps for commercial use," he said. "Commercial rearing is expected to begin sometime next year."
"Private companies can rear the parasite and sell it to the farmer," he said, adding there was a possibility the technology could be transferred to Indonesia.
In a report presented at the regional cocoa conference, Indonesia said about 42,000 hectares of its cocoa plantings had been infested by the pod borer.

A British entomologist is conducting field tests in the key growing region of South Sulawesi using a simple two-step technique that involves pruning the trees and regular harvesting that disrupts the life cycle of the pod borer moth.
Lee said the parasite being used in Malaysia could also help fight some insects that attack corn, vegetables and horticulture crops. "Its application can be much wider than just the pod borer.
"The use of the parasite is very environment friendly, and I feel this project has huge potential," he said, adding that using the parasite would cost less than spraying pesticide.

"In a small holding where 10 people are used to carry out the spraying, just one person is needed to release the parasite," he said. "It could also be a solution to the problem of recruiting people to work in Malaysian plantations."
